teaching.causalExplanation: Most covalent substances we've met so far are molecular. They're made of separate molecules, like carbon dioxide, with strong covalent bonds inside each molecule, and only weak attractions between the molecules. A covalent network is different. Covalent bonds join the atoms into one continuous structure, in layers or in 3D, right through the crystal. There are no separate molecules. So to melt it, you have to break covalent bonds, and that takes a lot of energy. A 3D network is also hard to scratch, for the same reason. Start with diamond. Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, to four other carbons, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, the shape we saw for methane. That pattern repeats in every direction, so a diamond is one giant 3D network. To scratch it, you'd have to break many strong bonds, so diamond is the hardest natural substance, a ten on the Mohs scale, which ranks minerals by which one scratches which. And all four outer electrons on each carbon are used in bonds, so none are free to move. Diamond doesn't conduct electricity. Graphite uses the same atoms differently. Each carbon bonds to only three others, in flat sheets of hexagons, like chicken wire. That leaves one outer electron on each carbon, and those electrons are delocalised, free to move along the whole sheet. So graphite conducts electricity along its layers. Between the sheets there are no covalent bonds, only weak attractions, so the sheets slide over each other easily. That's why graphite feels slippery, and why it rubs off as you write.

scenes.teachingReason: Start with diamond. Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, to four other carbons, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, the shape we saw for methane. That pattern repeats in every direction, so a diamond is one giant 3D network.
